title: The mustard seed again
hookLine: a mother goes door to door for one small seed, and every house answers
tomorrow: if grief comes from love, would loving less hurt less?

cards: Someone in a group chat writes that their dad died. The chat goes still. Then a message: my grandpa, last spring.
Then another: my aunt. Nobody fixes anything, and somehow the room gets less lonely. An old Buddhist story runs on the same strange arithmetic.
A young mother named Kisa Gotami has lost her little child. She can't accept it. She carries the child from house to house, asking everyone for medicine.
People turn her away, until someone sends her to the Buddha. He says he can help. Bring me one mustard seed, he says, from a house where nobody has died.

teach.b: Mustard seed is easy to find. Every kitchen has it. So she runs.
At the first door, they'd gladly give her seed, but they've lost a father. Next door, a sister. Next door, a son.
House after house, the seed is there, and the condition never is. The commentaries put a line in her neighbors' mouths that stays with you: the living are few, and the dead are many.
Somewhere along that street, something changes in her. She stops asking for medicine and starts hearing the stories. Notice what the Buddha doesn't do.
He never lectures her. He doesn't argue her out of grief or tell her to stop crying.
He sends her out to meet the neighbors, and the street does the teaching. She learns that death is in every house, and that she isn't the only one carrying this weight.
Tradition says she laid her child to rest, came back, became a nun, and later reached awakening. Her verses are among the poems of the early nuns.
Heard young, the story can sound like a trick: he knew there was no such seed.
Heard later in life, it sounds more like mercy. A teacher who knew no words would reach her, so he gave her a walk, and a whole town to keep her company.

how: Buddhist teachers retell Kisa Gotami's story at funerals and in talks on grief; in Theravada communities her verses are read among the Therigatha, the poems of the early nuns.

games.q: what does “the mustard seed again” mean?
o: a test the Buddha gave students to see who could keep a vow
a story about planting a tiny seed until it grows into a tree
a woman's search for a cure that taught her everyone loses someone

games.q: the story of the seed — tap the pairs.
p: a young mother who lost her child
seed from a house where nobody died
had seed, and had lost someone
the living are few, the dead many

s: in the story, the Buddha tells Kisa Gotami to stop grieving
he never lectures her. he sends her out, and the neighbors' stories do the teaching.
the seed itself was easy to find in every house
the seed was everywhere. the house without a death was nowhere.
the story is a trick to prove she was foolish
heard later in life it reads as mercy: a walk and a town's company, when words couldn't reach her.

games.q: a classmate's mom has died. you barely know them, and you've never lost a parent. a few people sit together at lunch, unsure. what does the seed story suggest?
o: say nothing; you haven't lost a parent, so it isn't your place.
sit with them, and let anyone who's lost someone say so, if they want.
give them space for a few weeks until they've had time to heal.
games.why: Kisa Gotami wasn't healed by an answer. she was met by a street full of people who had lost someone too. company did what argument couldn't.

practice: Look out a window, or down a street, or simply around the room you're in. Let your eyes rest on one door, one roof, one lit window at a time, and say silently: someone here has lost someone too.
Stay with the next one, and the next, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The mustard seed again: the story of Kisa Gotami, who went looking for a cure and found company. Death had visited every house on her street.

orig.note: Pali anicca: impermanent. what the whole street taught her without a sermon.

carryVoice: Keep this one: no house untouched, so grief is lonely and also on every street. Fourteen days into death and dying.
